name: Solder Paste

claims.claim_text: Paste application is the foundation of the whole assembly process. Without a good application there is no good reflow, and no amount of tuning the thermal profile afterwards will recover it.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you cannot get a good solder paste application, you cannot have a good reflow
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: Stated as a priority order: paste is by far the most critical step. However good the placement is, bad paste produces bad boards, which inverts where most beginners direct their attention.
claims.quote_verbatim: Paste is by far the most critical step of the process

claims.claim_text: A concrete cost of getting it wrong: two months of boards where nothing reflowed properly, traced to old paste kept out of frugality. Borrowing fresh paste fixed everything immediately, and yields in that period were around forty percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: our yields were about 40%, which is insanely low

claims.claim_text: The rule that follows is to use fresh paste every time and to check the stencil alignment carefully, because those two things dominate the outcome regardless of what the rest of the line is doing.
claims.quote_verbatim: always use fresh pace

claims.claim_text: Using long-expired paste is a recurring error even among experienced people. Five-year-old paste in a fridge is not usable stock, and the expiration dates on these products are firm rather than advisory.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was using five-year-old paste

claims.claim_text: The resulting discipline is to throw paste out regularly and buy new. There are many places in electronics where being frugal pays, and this is emphatically not one of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: solder paste is not one of those
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Expired paste does not stop working outright, it degrades: reflow gets worse, joints look bad and conductivity suffers, which makes the cause hard to identify because nothing fails cleanly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it becomes less and less effective

claims.claim_text: Bad paste has a recognisable physical signature. It cakes into something with the texture of material you could peel off a fingernail. It can sometimes be rescued on a hot plate with extra flux, but doing so is not good business.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like a cakes up
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: One particular paste is named repeatedly by people who assemble boards as having changed their results. The catch is packaging: it is sold in tubes of five or six hundred grams, so the cost per gram is low but the entry cost is not.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to buy a large quantity
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: The same product is reported to remain usable well past its rated one-year life, which is the exception that proves the rule about fresh paste rather than a licence to keep any paste indefinitely.
claims.quote_verbatim: it stays past their expiration date
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: The combined recommendation for anyone struggling with reflow is to change two things at once: move to a framed stencil and switch to known-good paste. Those two changes address most of what goes wrong before the oven.
claims.quote_verbatim: go to a frame, stencil and start using GC 10
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: What paste physically is explains its behaviour: a slurry of tacky flux and powdered solder. The tackiness is load-bearing, because it holds every placed component in position until reflow.
claims.quote_verbatim: paste is a slurry of, of kind of tacky flux and, uh, powdered metal
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: The machine sequence runs in one direction: a stencil printer aligns the stencil to the board and prints the paste, that printer feeds the placement machine which sets parts onto the tacky deposits, and the board then passes into a reflow oven that melts everything on a tightly controlled ramp.
claims.quote_verbatim: you print the solder paste onto the circuit board
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A stencil is exactly what the name suggests: a mask ensuring paste lands only on the copper pads. Its purpose is the right amount of paste in the right places consistently, rather than the inconsistency of dabbing it on by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want to create a mask between the board and essentially your solder paste
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Paste is shear-thinning, which is why technique matters. Good paste becomes thinner while being spread and firms up again once the stroke stops, and that recovery is what produces the tack that holds parts. Components should not be placed onto paste that is still liquid.
claims.quote_verbatim: the viscosity on good quality paste will get thinner so that it's easier to spread
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: The technique rule that follows is counterintuitive: use the smallest pressure that will distribute paste evenly across the stencil in a single pass. Pressing harder makes the result worse rather than more complete.
claims.quote_verbatim: apply the smallest amount of pressure possible
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Stencil aperture quality has a direct effect on release. A smooth, almost flame-polished interior lets paste leave the aperture cleanly, while a jagged cut edge holds onto it, and clogging with old paste is the main thing that degrades a stencil over its life.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the biggest enemies to a stencil is clogging
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Clogging works by narrowing the aperture, which reduces the volume of paste deposited and produces exactly the defects associated with too little paste, tombstoning among them. A stencil that once worked can therefore start producing faults without anything else changing.
claims.quote_verbatim: it shrinks up that hole so that then you have, you apply less paste
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Production engineers routinely modify individual apertures rather than accepting a defect. If one component consistently tombstones, they will have a stencil made with a larger opening at that pad so it receives more paste.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll go get a new stencil that opens up the pad
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: The reason that adjustment is needed is mechanical. An automated squeegee makes one pass at nominally constant pressure, and pads earlier in the stroke can absorb a clump of paste, leaving later pads slightly starved. Opening those apertures compensates for the position rather than the pad.
claims.quote_verbatim: the two pads just above yours might have absorbed, you know, a big clump of pace
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Tombstoning has several independent causes and diagnosing it means checking all of them: a mismatch between the part, the paste volume and the pad geometry, the reflow profile itself, and thermal asymmetry where one pad connects to a ground plane and therefore heats and cools differently from the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: mismatching for the part relative to the solder paste relative to the pads
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: A via inside a pad wicks paste away down the hole by capillary action, starving the joint of solder. This is the hidden cost of putting vias in pads when there was no room to route them out.
claims.quote_verbatim: it can suck away all of your solder paste
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The dominant error in hand application is using too much paste. Only a small amount is needed to make a connection, and excess is what produces bridges, so the instinct to be generous is precisely wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: not using too much

claims.claim_text: Under a ball grid array that error becomes serious, because the resulting shorts are underneath the package where they cannot be seen. You will never find them by inspection.
claims.quote_verbatim: You'll never find them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Reflowing a ball grid array is more forgiving than its reputation suggests, because the process is self-aligning: surface tension pulls the package into position. A cheap mylar stencil and the correct paste volume are enough to make it work.
claims.quote_verbatim: The surface tension, you know, pulls the chip in line

claims.claim_text: For a fine-pitch quad flat pack there is no need to place paste on each pad individually. Laying a single line of paste across the whole row works, because the solder mask and surface tension sort it out during reflow without bridging.
claims.quote_verbatim: You just do a line across

claims.claim_text: That is what solder mask is for, and it is also why paste volume matters more than precision: put too much on and the mask cannot prevent bridging however well the stencil was aligned.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the magic of soda mask and the amount of paste you put on
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Placement accuracy requirements are more relaxed than they appear, because parts wiggle back into position under surface tension as the solder melts. For ordinary passives the tolerance of the paste deposit is what matters, not the placement.
claims.quote_verbatim: it kind of wiggles back into place
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: A workable home stencilling setup: surround the board with spare boards of the same thickness so the surface is level, tape the stencil down along one edge, lay a bead of paste along the top and squeegee with a stainless blade.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's a common technique to use spare PCBs cause then they're all the same thickness
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: The traditional advice to squeegee in one single stroke is worth testing rather than obeying. One practitioner gets better results with a stroke down, a stroke back up, and a final pass at a sharp angle to scrape the surface clean.
claims.quote_verbatim: one squeegee down from the top and then, uh, up from the bottom
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: Stated at its simplest, the method is a blank board to sit the work in, the stencil on top, and an old credit card to draw the paste across. Getting the surrounding surface flush with the board is the part that matters.
claims.quote_verbatim: You get a blank piece of PCB and then you just stick your stencil on top

claims.claim_text: For very small boards even a stencil can be improvised: two strips of tape either side acting as shims to set the thickness, then a credit card skimmed along them to leave an even layer.
claims.quote_verbatim: lay down two strips of scotch tape
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: The accessibility argument for paste is that people assume surface-mount work requires a soldering iron, which is genuinely hard, and are surprised how much easier paste methods are. Demonstrating a reflow over a candle flame makes the point that the process is more approachable than the equipment implies.
claims.quote_verbatim: how scrappy can we get with, with that method
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: Printed paste has a working window. Once it is on the board the assembly needs to reach the oven within a few hours, so populated boards cannot be left sitting overnight waiting for the rest of a panel to be finished.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to put it in the oven within like four hours
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: At the low-cost end of dispensing, an air-compressor syringe dispenser is likely to fail quickly because of its seals, while a mechanical lever press gives slow controlled dispensing calibrated to the hand and has nothing to wear out.
claims.quote_verbatim: the $100 one is probably going to break in about a day
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: At the other end, dispensing machines plot paste dot by dot with an XY head rather than squeegeeing through a stencil, achieving high accuracy at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: they squirt out solder paste with like an actual XY plotter

claims.claim_text: Assembly houses have been moving from stencils to paste printers for speed rather than quality. A printer removes the wait for a stencil to be made and shipped, which matters most for high-mix work where fifteen designs in a day would otherwise need fifteen stencils.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was because of the speed
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Component size feeds directly into assembly price. Smaller parts cannot be jet-printed and require finer, more expensive stencils, which is one of the specific ways that going outside the normal envelope starts to incur cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: the smaller, the component, the more difficult it is to print solder paste
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A failure worth recognising: an entire region of a panel came out unpopulated, which looked like a placement problem and turned out to be paste never having been scraped across that part of the panel at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no paste down there

claims.claim_text: Paste tack does mechanical work during placement. The board flexes as the nozzle presses a part down and springs back as it releases, and it is the tack of the paste that keeps the component from being flicked off the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the tension of your solder paste is supposed to keep the part there

claims.claim_text: The most sophisticated factories treat paste as a tracked material like any component: which lot it came from, when it was taken out to come up to temperature, and the hours during which it was used, all recorded against the boards it was used on.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'd know this was from this lot
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Paste application can dominate the yield of a hand-built board outright. One builder got a single working board out of five, which was the reason for moving the design from a ball grid array to a leaded package that could be inspected and reworked.
claims.quote_verbatim: I only got one to work with my terrible solder paste application

claims.claim_text: On a milled board there is no solder mask to contain the paste, so reflow depends on flux behaviour alone and bridging is much more likely. By the time the machine is set up to dispense, hand soldering the board would often have been faster.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have the the solder mask then to kind of help guide it along
claims.episode_title: Glass and Gongkai GSM - Unzymotic Ursidae Upbuilding

claims.claim_text: Stencils stopped being a cost barrier once fabricators began cutting them from mylar in seconds and including them with the boards, which is what made stencilled application practical for one-off prototypes.
claims.quote_verbatim: They cut them out of mylar these days
